source.version: ACM version of record, CI '25: Proceedings of the ACM Collective Intelligence Conference, printed pp. 297-316, published 4 August 2025 (CC BY 4.0); ACM Digital Library download cover page dated 16 December 2025 is PDF p. 1. PDF page = printed page minus 295.
source.title_on_document: Cueing the Crowd: LLM-Driven Conversational Cues Across Different Meeting Modalities Increase Topical Diversity of Generated Ideas

supplement.where: Appendix A.1 'Supplemental Materials': https://osf.io/nmqd5/files/osfstorage?view_only=0b6efc5a1bf3466395292501cd52de2f (PDF p. 15, printed p. 310)
supplement.holds: The paper describes it as 'The data for this project'. The appendix itself (task instructions, prompts, homogenization method, surveys) is in this PDF. No statistics are said to sit only in the supplement.

paper_design_summary: 172 participants (mostly students earning course credit) worked in 86 dyads on a 20-minute verbal brainstorming task (alternative uses for recyclable trash from a beach cleanup) in a 2x2 between-subjects lab experiment: dyads either received a GPT-4o-mini-generated conversational cue about once per minute (CueTip) or no cues, and talked either in person or virtually. The authors scored the dyad's ideas for topic diversity (BERTopic clusters with Shannon entropy), counted ideas, scored the conversation transcript for the number of unique topics, and compared the cosine distance of each idea to its condition's average embedding (homogenization). A post-study, model-only analysis compared the diversity of the original cues with cues regenerated by a Wikipedia-based pipeline.

studies.label: 2x2 lab experiment: AI conversational cues (Cue vs NoCue) x modality (in-person vs virtual), dyadic brainstorming

assignment.what_was_assigned: One of four conditions: Cue-Virtual, Cue-InPerson, NoCue-Virtual, NoCue-InPerson. The paper says participants were randomly assigned; both members of a dyad share one condition, and the analyses are at the dyad level.
assignment.quote: We recruited 172 participants, randomly assigned to four conditions; Cue-Virtual, Cue-InPerson, NoCue-Virtual, and NoCue-InPerson to participate in a brainstorming discussion with one other participant (in 86 dyads).
assignment.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 300), Sec. 4.1.1; also Sec. 4 opening (PDF p. 5) and Sec. 8 (PDF p. 11)

arms.name: Cue-Virtual
arms.description: Dyad in separate rooms over the CueTip video call; GPT-4o-mini cue (at most five words) delivered about once per minute with a visual notification and audio chime

arms.name: Cue-InPerson
arms.description: Dyad in the same room, each on a laptop running CueTip; same cue delivery as Cue-Virtual

arms.name: NoCue-Virtual
arms.description: Dyad in separate rooms over the video call with shared notes; no cues

arms.name: NoCue-InPerson
arms.description: Dyad in the same room with shared notes; no cues

participants.exclusions: Two discussions were removed for echoes in the audio recordings and two other sessions were dropped for technical issues (4 dyads); the paper does not state the resulting number of participants or dyads analyzed. Thirteen participants who did not report prior design experience and topic knowledge were excluded from analyses that accounted for these factors (the REML models include them as random effects). For the conversation analysis, footnote 12 says audio came from 70 sessions, of which 4 were excluded for echoes and 16 were not included because the recorder captured only the researcher. Two sessions were excluded from the cue-noticing coding. Per-arm counts are not reported.
participants.who: Participants aged 18 to 37 (median 21), 42 male, 127 female, 3 non-binary; compensated with course credit or $20 for 75 minutes; the authors say almost all were psychology or cognitive science students.
participants.country: not stated (lab study run by a UC San Diego team)
participants.quote: A majority of the participants in our study participated for research credit. This may have contributed to a selection bias because almost all of the participants were in psychology or cognitive science.
participants.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 300), Sec. 4.1.1; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 306), Sec. 7; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), footnote 12

ai_tool.name_model: CueTip system using OpenAI GPT-4o-mini; real-time transcription from Daily.js
ai_tool.how_used: Cues were generated automatically from the conversation summary and the last ten utterances and pushed to the dyad about once per minute (18 +/- 2 cues per 20-minute session), prompted to be at most five words and to encourage divergence (e.g., 'What if we created furniture?'). Participants could not query the model; they could read the current cue and the cue history.

task.description: Dyadic verbal brainstorming: come up with as many alternative uses as possible to repurpose recyclable trash uncovered during a beach cleanup, writing ideas as bullet points in shared notes; first 15 minutes generating, last 5 minutes selecting the best idea. Preceded by a familiarity-building task.

outcomes.name: Topic diversity of generated ideas (dyad level)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Ideas pooled across all groups and fit with BERTopic using HDBSCAN clustering (minimum cluster size 15); Shannon entropy (scipy) computed as the topic diversity score. The paper says entropy gives 'each idea's topic diversity score' but analyzes one score per dyad (Fig. 5a). Coded as flexibility because it measures topical variety within one dyad's own ideas, not similarity across dyads. The text of Sec. 5.1.1 says 'The topic diversity of cues served as the dependent variable', apparently a slip for ideas.

contrasts.reported: REML with Access-to-Cue x Modality fixed effects, prior design experience and recycling knowledge random effects: Access-to-Cue F(1, 67.03) = 6.51, p = 0.013; cues (mu = 2.3, SD = 0.3) vs without cues (mu = 2.1, SD = 0.4); modality F(1, 67.17) = 0.79, p = 0.38; no interaction; Tukey HSD p ~ 0.012. Fig. 5a box plot: Cue median 2.351 (Q1 2.095, Q3 2.525); Without Cue median 2.098 (Q1 1.839, Q3 2.322). Group counts per arm not reported.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), Sec. 5.1.1; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 303), Fig. 5a

outcomes.name: Homogenization of ideas: cosine distance of each idea to its condition's average idea embedding
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Following Anderson, Shah and Kreminski (2024): average embedding of all ideas within each condition (Cue, NoCue), then cosine distance (scikit-learn pairwise distances) between that average and each idea; distributions compared with a Wilcoxon test. Higher distance = more varied ideas across groups.

contrasts.reported: No test statistic, p-value, mean, or n is printed for ideas. The text says a Wilcoxon test was conducted and then reports only that 'across groups, participants were exposed to semantically similar cues' (182 of 578 divergence cues repeated verbatim in other groups). Fig. 6 violin plots of cosine distance show medians near 0.55 for both Cue Ideas and No Cue Ideas; the caption says a more concentrated distribution indicates lower semantic variability but does not say which arm is more concentrated. Direction coded from the figure; the paper states none.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 306), Sec. 6.3; PDF p. 16 (printed p. 311), App. A.4.1; PDF p. 17 (printed p. 312), Fig. 6

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine distance between each idea embedding and the average embedding of all ideas in the same condition
diversity_detail.computed_over: each output against the condition's centroid (average embedding of all ideas within the condition, pooled across dyads)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Wilcoxon test on idea-level distances (result not reported for ideas)
diversity_detail.notes: The intro (PDF p. 3) states that cues led to more topically diverse ideation within groups but that 'we observe a homogenization effect across groups where similar cues are generated for group after group'; that claim is about the cues, not tested on ideas in the text.

outcomes.name: Topic diversity of the conversation transcript (number of unique IAB Level 1 topics)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Ideation conversation audio transcribed with AssemblyAI; utterances mapped to the 698 Interactive Advertising Bureau topics; score = combined set of unique Level 1 topics across all rounds of the dyad's conversation. Scored on the spoken discussion, not on the written ideas.

contrasts.reported: REML: Access-to-Cue F(1, 50.76) = 6.25, p = 0.016; cues (mu = 9.6, SD = 2.2) vs without cues (mu = 8.0, SD = 2.5); modality F(1, 50.79) = 0.25, p = 0.62; no interaction; Tukey HSD p ~ 0.015. Fig. 5b: Cue median 9.00 (Q1 7.50, Q3 11.00); Without Cue median 8.00 (Q1 6.00, Q3 9.00).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 9 (printed p. 304), Sec. 5.1.2; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 303), Fig. 5b; PDF p. 7, footnote 12

outcomes.name: Number of ideas per dyad
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Research team de-duplicated the raw notes, filled in missing ideas from recordings and transcripts, and counted points per session. Dyads averaged 19.4 ideas overall.

contrasts.reported: 'None of the factors showed a significant difference based on the REML model.' No arm means, test statistics, or p-values printed. Overall mean 19.4 ideas per dyad.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 9 (printed p. 304), Sec. 5.1.3; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), Sec. 5

studies.label: Post-study cue-generation analysis: original zero-shot cues vs Wikipedia-based pipeline cues (no participants)

assignment.quote: To evaluate this approach, we compared the original set of cues from the study against new cues generated by our revised pipeline

arms.name: Pipeline cues
arms.description: Cues regenerated for the same transcripts using Wikipedia 'See Also' entities as input

participants.who: No human participants; AI-generated cues only.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4o-mini (study cues) and a revised Wikipedia-based prompting pipeline
ai_tool.how_used: Model output only; no person used it.

task.description: Generation of brainstorming cues for the beach-cleanup alternative-uses task

outcomes.name: Cosine distance of each cue to the average cue embedding
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: AI-generated cues, not participant output. Wilcoxon test on cue version.

contrasts.reported: Cues without the pipeline (mu = 0.46, SD = 0.11) significantly (p < 0.0001) more homogeneous than with the pipeline (mu = 0.54, SD = 0.23). Counts of cues per version not printed. Study cues: 578 divergence cues, 182 repeated verbatim in one or more other groups.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 306), Sec. 6.3; PDF p. 19 (printed p. 314), Fig. 10

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine distance between each cue embedding and the average embedding of cues within its version
diversity_detail.computed_over: each cue against its version's centroid
diversity_detail.notes: Model-only; does not enter the core dataset.

company_involvement.description: Funded by the National Science Foundation (grant #2009003); no company authors or funders stated. Uses OpenAI GPT-4o-mini as a tool.

eligibility.reason: S1 randomly assigned 172 participants (86 dyads) to receive GPT-4o-mini conversational cues or no cues during a brainstorming task (p. 300, Sec. 4.1.1). The analyzed count is not stated; 4 dyads were dropped and the conversation analysis used fewer sessions, but every stated count stays well above 50 people. Outcomes are scored on the dyads' ideas and conversation (topic diversity, idea count, idea-to-centroid cosine distance). Assignment and analysis are at the dyad level, so the number of independent units is roughly 70 to 86 dyads.

one_line_finding: Dyads that received GPT-4o-mini cues produced more topically diverse ideas (entropy mean 2.3 vs 2.1; F(1, 67.03) = 6.51, p = 0.013) and conversations (9.6 vs 8.0 unique topics; F(1, 50.76) = 6.25, p = 0.016) but not more ideas, with no modality effect (PDF pp. 7-9, Sec. 5.1).
open_questions: Analyzed sample size is not stated: 86 dyads were assigned, 4 sessions were dropped, but footnote 12 refers to a total of 70 sessions of audio; the REML denominator df (67.03 for ideas, 50.76 for conversation) suggest roughly 70 and 50 dyads.
The homogenization (across-dyad) test on ideas is described but no result is printed; Fig. 6 is the only evidence and the caption does not say which arm is more concentrated.
Whether within-dyad topic entropy of ideas should be coded as flexibility (variety within one team's ideas) or as diversity; the paper calls it 'topic diversity'.
Sec. 5.1.1 names 'the topic diversity of cues' as the dependent variable, which appears to be a typo for ideas.
Whether conversation-transcript topic diversity counts as an outcome scored on the output.
notes: Paper also reports correlational (non-randomized) analyses within cued dyads: the number of cues a dyad attended to correlated with idea topic diversity (Spearman p ~ 0.024, r_s ~ 0.35) and, in virtual groups only, with number of ideas (p ~ 0.0024, r_s ~ 0.63) (PDF p. 9, Sec. 5.2). Cue noticing: InPerson mean 15.0 (SD 3.1) vs Virtual 14.2 (SD 4.2), Wilcoxon p ~ 0.88. Modality contrasts (in-person vs virtual) are not AI contrasts and are omitted as separate outcomes. The authors note they did not use expert ratings of novelty, creativity, or feasibility because of the large number of ideas (PDF p. 7, Sec. 5.1). Post-survey items are self-reports and are not listed. A 10-person (5-dyad) pilot preceded the study (PDF p. 4, Sec. 3.1).
